sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** No. Two optional fields serve the company, not the person signing up: "Workspace name" (≈436–844 × 485–551) and "How did you hear about us?" (≈436–844 × 570–636). They make the form six fields instead of four, and they sit between the password field and the button. Someone who just wants to try a notes app has to scroll past two more boxes and decide whether to skip them. The select box makes this worse: it shows no prompt and no "(optional)" label, so it looks unfinished and makes the viewer stop to think. Nielsen's heuristic 8 (aesthetic and minimalist design) says every element on the screen should support the user's main task. The marketing question does not. The fix is to take "How did you hear about us?" off the signup and ask it after the account exists, or drop it. The workspace name could be filled in by default (for example "Ben's notes") so it doesn't need to be asked, or asked on the first screen after signup. If both stay, mark them "(optional)" and put them below a clear break so the four required fields read as the form. Convention. Weight: minor. The form still works, but it is longer than the task needs.
2. **(No checklist line for this; it's about the copy.)** "Create your account / Start a free workspace for your notes." could be the signup page of any notes app. Together with the stock blue-on-pale-blue card, nothing on the page says why Quillnest and not the notes tool the viewer already uses. That doesn't stop someone who has already decided to sign up. It does nothing for someone still deciding. The direction of the fix is to make the subhead name the one thing Quillnest does differently, in the viewer's terms. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **The purpose is clear in a second.** The bold headline at the top of a single centred card, with the full-width dark-blue "Create account" button at the bottom, tells a first-time viewer exactly what the page is for and how to finish.
- **It reads as one piece.** One typeface, one blue used for the logo, the button and the focus colour, and the same rounded corners on the card, inputs and button all belong to the same calm style, which suits a notes tool.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether "Sign in" (≈700–742, 731) is actually a link: it's the same grey as the sentence around it. That belongs to the Interface section, but it decides whether returning users can find their way out of this page.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (every element does a job)

I worked through the hierarchy section for the sign-up card. The image is one screen (1280×800), so I didn't crop it and worked from the whole image. All type sizes below are estimates by eye, since there was no measured facts file.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?"** No, on the size part.
   - **Where:** the regular grey text appears in three sizes that are almost the same:
     - the subtitle "Start a free workspace for your notes." (436,165) looks about 15 px;
     - the "* Required field" note (436,201) looks about 13 px;
     - the footer "Already have an account? Sign in" (538–742, 731) looks about 13 px.
   - **Also:** the bold field labels ("First name", "Email address"…) look about 14 px, so four text sizes sit within about two pixels of each other.
   - **What the viewer meets:** weight and colour still separate labels from helper text, so the form reads. But the subtitle and the small grey notes look like the same kind of text at a slightly different size. To the eye they are neither the same level nor clearly different ones, so the subtitle, which is the only line that says what the product gives you, doesn't stand out from the fine print.
   - **Why:** sizes should come from a small, deliberate scale (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1, p. 45). A difference of one step looks like an accident, not a choice (Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8).
   - **Fix:** use fewer sizes with bigger steps. One body size (about 15–16 px) for the subtitle, labels and the footer link, with weight and colour doing the work. Keep one clearly smaller size for the required-field note only, or drop that note, since the red asterisks already say it.
   - **Type and weight:** convention. Minor.

**What's working.**
- **The heading and the button bracket the task.** "Create your account" is the largest, darkest type, at the top of the card. The solid full-width blue "Create account" button is the heaviest mass, at the bottom. The eye starts at the title, runs down the fields and lands on the action, which is the right order for a sign-up.
- **Labels stand apart from the fields by weight and colour, not size.** The bold, near-black labels sit above pale-bordered inputs, so each label-and-field pair reads as one unit without extra sizes. This is "bolder, not bigger" (Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*).

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (each text level distinct with no two sizes almost the same)

The walk is finished and I've checked the grouping rule. Here's the report.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** No, in one place. The "* Required field" note (about y 195–207, x 436) sits roughly 25 px below the subtitle and roughly 28 px above the "First name" label, so it's about the same distance from both. It belongs to neither the header ("Create your account" and the subtitle) nor the form. The reader sees it as a third, separate line and has to work out that it explains the red asterisks below. When the gaps on both sides are equal, the grouping disappears (Wertheimer's proximity rule, as in Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II). **Fix:** attach it to the form. Open up the gap between the subtitle and the note, and close the gap between the note and the first label so it clearly sits with the fields. Or move the note to just above or below the button. **Type:** convention. **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- **One clean column grid.** Every field, the select and the button share the same edges at x 436 and 844. The first and last name row splits that column into two equal halves with a narrow gutter, and their labels and inputs line up across. The form reads as one firm stack, and the eye runs straight down it to the button.
- **Label and field spacing.** Each label sits about 8 px above its input, and the gap to the next label is about 20 px. Every label clearly belongs to its own field.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (space inside groups smaller than between groups)

Walk (Text, working notes): body/subtitle ~15 px yes; labels/helper ~12–13 px yes; plain upright sans yes; one family (Inter-like) yes; small text in medium/semibold yes; contrast: slate helper and grey "Already have an account? Sign in" look ≥4.5:1 on white, yes; no text over images yes; no paragraphs, so measure, leading, multi-line heading, alignment, justification, rag, widows, paragraph marks, hanging punctuation, chunking all yes; mixed case yes; emphasis yes; heading spacing and kerning look fine at a close crop, yes; tracking yes; no caps strings yes; no fi/fl in large type yes; no faux styles yes; "?" and "*" only, no quotes or dashes, yes; no number columns yes; real type yes; nothing clipped yes. No lines answered no or unsure, so I don't need to open any entries.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Clean type scale:** I count four sizes: the heading (~26 px bold), the subtitle (~15 px regular), the labels (~14 px semibold), and the helper and footer lines (~13 px). Each one has its own job, and labels are told apart from helper text by weight rather than by another size. That's the "bolder, not bigger" approach from Refactoring UI. Keep it to these four sizes when you revise.
- **Small text stays readable:** "* Required field" (y≈201) and "Already have an account? Sign in" (y≈731) are small, but they use a solid weight in a dark slate grey, not a pale grey. They stay readable on white, so the bottom line of the form doesn't fade away.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

The color review is done; the report follows.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each color that is meant to match look the same wherever it sits?** No. The asterisk in the "* Required field" key (about x 436, y 201) is the same slate gray as the key's text. The asterisks it explains, next to First name, Last name, Email address and Password (x 511–540, y 237–407), are red. A key is supposed to look exactly like the marks it explains. Here someone has to make the link by shape alone. The cost is small because the asterisk is a familiar mark, but it makes the form look a little less finished. The "Simultaneous contrast" entry covers colors that only look different because of what surrounds them. This is a real color mismatch, so it rests on common sense rather than on a source. Fix: make the key's asterisk the same red as the field asterisks. Taste. Minor.

**What's working.**
- **Restrained palette with a clear light-to-dark range.** The page uses one blue for the brand, shared by the logo and the "Create account" button, plus navy text, gray-blue field borders, a white card on a pale blue-gray background, and red only for the asterisks. The button is the only large block of strong color, so it is clearly the one action on the page. The navy text against white and the dark button against the pale background keep the page's structure clear even in grayscale.
- **Red used for its usual meaning.** On a form, red means "required" or "error", and here it appears only on the required-field asterisks. That keeps it free to carry error states later without clashing with anything else.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (matching colors look the same: the key's asterisk is gray, the field asterisks are red).

**Section.** Pictures: applies, but only through the "Quillnest" wordmark at the top left (about x 56–143, y 22–42). The screen has no photos, illustrations or icons. The dropdown chevron is a native control and belongs to Interface.

None.

sections.report:
I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts because Bash was denied. I read the reference entries directly instead.

**Section.** Interface: applies. This is a single-screen sign-up form with six fields, one primary button and one link.

**Findings**
1. **"Does every control look like what it does… and links marked by more than color?"** The "Sign in" link in "Already have an account? Sign in" (around 700,731) is the same small grey as the rest of the sentence. It has no underline, no colour change and no weight change, so it looks like plain text. A returning user who landed here by mistake has to guess where to click to get out. That is the only exit from this flow, which makes it the wrong place to hide. Under WCAG G183/F73, an inline link needs at least 3:1 colour contrast with the text around it, plus a non-colour cue; an underline by default is safest. Fix: underline "Sign in" or put it in the brand blue (or both), and make the whole phrase the link target. **Defect / convention. Weight: minor.**
2. **"Do input borders, control edges, and meaningful icons reach 3:1 contrast against what is next to them?"** The borders on all six fields (x 436–844, y 254–636) look like a light slate on white. By eye that is about #94A3B8, which would be roughly 2.5:1, below the 3:1 that WCAG 1.4.11 asks for. The fields have no fill, so the border is the only thing that shows where you type. Low-vision users will see faint boxes or none. Measure the computed border colour. If it comes in under 3:1, darken it one step (to about slate-500) or give the fields a light fill. **Convention (WCAG 1.4.11). Weight: minor.**
3. **"Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them…?"** The "How did you hear about us?" select (436–844, 594–636) is empty. It shows no "Select one" prompt and no default, just a blank box with a chevron. It looks unfinished, and it doesn't tell the user that this question is optional or what the choices are until they open it. "Workspace name" is also blank, even though it could be filled from the user's first name (for example "Ben's notes"). Fix: give the select a "Select an option (optional)" placeholder and prefill the workspace name. **Defect. Weight: minor.**
4. **"Are rare or advanced options kept behind a visible control, with the main content first?"** Two optional fields that don't help the user sign up sit in the main path: "Workspace name" and a marketing question, "How did you hear about us?". They make the form about a third longer and add steps before the one button that matters. For a free notes app, the cost of signing up is the thing that decides whether someone finishes. Fix: move both to the first screen after the account exists (onboarding), or drop the marketing question. **Taste (common sense about signup friction; I couldn't open the catalog entry). Weight: major.** This is the main thing standing between the form and its job of short, low-friction sign-up.
5. **"Where the task is complex, is short help shown near the step it concerns?"** The Password field (424–466) gives no rules: no minimum length, no character requirements. Users find out only from an error after they submit, and with no show/hide control they can't check a mistyped password either. "Workspace name" also comes with no explanation of what a workspace is or whether it can be changed later. Fix: put one line of help under Password (for example "At least 8 characters") and a short hint under Workspace name if you keep that field. **Defect. Weight: minor.**
6. **"Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know from the platform and similar products?"** The Password field has no show/hide toggle. Sign-up forms commonly have one, and it matters most here because there is no confirm field. Fix: add an eye toggle inside the field on the right. **Convention. Weight: minor.**

**What's working.**
- There is exactly one primary action. "Create account" is the only filled, high-contrast element on the card and spans the full width of the fields, so the next step is never in question.
- Every field has its own bold label directly above it, closer to its field than to the one above. Required fields have a red asterisk, and the "* Required field" key explains it up front. First/last name is the only side-by-side pair, and it is a short related pair, as it should be.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicator. On a keyboard-driven form, check that each field and the button show a ring at least 2 px thick with 3:1 contrast.
- Input types. Check that Email uses `type=email` and Password uses `type=password` with autocomplete hints, so phones show the right keyboard and password managers fill the fields.
- Error states. Check that errors name the field in words and say how to fix them.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 25 yes, 6 no (links marked by more than color; input borders 3:1; anticipate what's needed next; rare options behind a control; short help near the step; platform conventions), 2 unsure (focus indicator; inputs allow only valid values)
